header:
How the stock market
actually works

lines.text: Most U.S. stock trading never touches a stock exchange.
lines.say: Most US stock trading never touches a stock exchange.

lines.text: In 2025, 50.6% of share volume traded away from exchanges like the NYSE and Nasdaq. A first, per Cboe.
lines.say: In twenty twenty-five, fifty point six percent of share volume traded away from exchanges like the N Y S E and Nasdaq. That's a first, according to Cboe.

lines.text: So where does it go? And who decides the price you pay?
lines.say: So where does it go? And who decides the price you pay?

lines.text: And that matters. In 2022, 58% of U.S. families owned stock, directly or through funds or retirement plans.
lines.say: And that matters. In twenty twenty-two, fifty-eight percent of US families owned stock, directly or through funds or retirement plans.

lines.text: A record in the Fed's survey, up from 52.6% in 2019.
lines.say: A record in the Fed's survey, up from fifty-two point six percent in twenty nineteen.

lines.text: So what actually happens after you tap buy? By the end of this video, you'll know.
lines.say: So what actually happens after you tap buy? By the end of this video, you'll know.

lines.text: The plan: what you own, where trades go, how prices form, and the scoreboard and rules.
lines.say: The plan: what you own, where trades go, how prices form, and the scoreboard and rules.

lines.text: Education, not advice: no stock picks, no predictions. Just how the machine works.
lines.say: Education, not advice: no stock picks, no predictions. Just how the machine works.

lines.text: Chapter 1: What you actually own.
lines.say: Chapter one: what you actually own.

lines.text: A share is a tiny slice of ownership in a company. Own one, and you own a sliver of the business.
lines.say: A share is a tiny slice of ownership in a company. Own one, and you own a sliver of the whole business.

lines.text: Multiply the share price by the number of shares, and you get the company's total value, called market cap.
lines.say: Multiply the share price by the number of shares, and you get the company's total value. That's called its market cap.

lines.text: Example: a made-up company has 1,000,000 shares at $50 each. That's a $50,000,000 market cap.
lines.say: Here's an example. A made-up company has one million shares at fifty dollars each. That's a fifty million dollar market cap.

lines.text: If the price ticks up to $51, the market cap becomes $51,000,000. That's $1,000,000 more, on paper.
lines.say: If the price ticks up to fifty-one dollars, the market cap becomes fifty-one million. That's one million dollars more, on paper.

lines.text: Here's the twist: the company didn't get a cent of that extra million. Investors just traded with each other.
lines.say: Here's the twist. The company didn't get a cent of that extra million. Investors just traded with each other.

lines.text: That's the big split. In an IPO, the company sells new shares and keeps the cash. After that, investors trade with each other.
lines.say: That's the big split. In an initial public offering, or I P O, the company sells new shares and keeps the cash. After that, investors trade with each other.

lines.text: In 2025, 202 U.S. IPOs raised $44.0 billion combined, a four-year high, per Renaissance Capital.
lines.say: In twenty twenty-five, two hundred two US I P Os raised forty-four billion dollars combined, a four-year high, according to Renaissance Capital.

lines.text: The biggest was Medline, which raised $6.3 billion, the largest U.S. IPO since 2021.
lines.say: The biggest was Medline, which raised six point three billion dollars, the largest US I P O since twenty twenty-one.

lines.text: The share count can change, too. In June 2024, Nvidia split each share into 10. More slices, same pizza.
lines.say: The share count can change, too. In June twenty twenty-four, Nvidia split each share into ten. More slices, same pizza.

lines.text: So a stock price alone tells you very little. $50 a share means nothing until you know how many shares exist.
lines.say: So a stock price on its own tells you very little. Fifty dollars a share means nothing until you know how many shares exist.

lines.text: Add up every company, and the U.S. stock market was worth $68.9 trillion in 2025, 43.7% of the world's total, per SIFMA.
lines.say: Add up every company, and the US stock market was worth sixty-eight point nine trillion dollars in twenty twenty-five. That's forty-three point seven percent of the world's total, according to SIFMA.

lines.text: That made it 4.4 times the size of China's, the next biggest stock market.
lines.say: That made it four point four times the size of China's, the next biggest stock market.

lines.text: Chapter 2: Where trades happen.
lines.say: Chapter two: where trades happen.

lines.text: It started, more or less, under a tree. On May 17, 1792, 24 brokers signed the Buttonwood Agreement in New York.
lines.say: It started, more or less, under a tree. On May seventeenth, seventeen ninety-two, twenty-four brokers signed the Buttonwood Agreement in New York.

lines.text: That deal grew into the New York Stock Exchange. Then on Feb. 8, 1971, Nasdaq opened as the world's first electronic stock market.
lines.say: That deal grew into the New York Stock Exchange. Then, on February eighth, nineteen seventy-one, Nasdaq opened as the world's first electronic stock market.

lines.text: An exchange is basically a giant matching engine: buy orders on one side, sell orders on the other, paired up by computer.
lines.say: An exchange is basically a giant matching engine. Buy orders on one side, sell orders on the other, paired up by computer.

lines.text: The regular session runs 9:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. Eastern, Monday through Friday, minus holidays.
lines.say: The regular session runs from nine thirty A M to four P M Eastern, Monday through Friday, minus holidays.

lines.text: In 2026, for example, markets close for Thanksgiving on Nov. 26, then close early, at 1 p.m., the day after.
lines.say: In twenty twenty-six, for example, markets close for Thanksgiving on November twenty-sixth, then close early, at one P M, the day after.

lines.text: And those hours are set to stretch. On April 10, 2026, the SEC approved Nasdaq's plan to trade 23 hours a day, five days a week.
lines.say: And those hours are set to stretch. On April tenth, twenty twenty-six, the S E C approved Nasdaq's plan to trade twenty-three hours a day, five days a week.

scene.headline: SEC approves Nasdaq plan for 23-hour trading

lines.text: As of September 2026, Nasdaq and NYSE Arca planned a new overnight session, 9 p.m. to 4 a.m. Eastern, starting Dec. 6, 2026.
lines.say: As of September twenty twenty-six, Nasdaq and N Y S E Arca planned a new overnight session, from nine P M to four A M Eastern, starting December sixth, twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: Why? Demand for U.S. stocks from overseas, and competition from crypto platforms that never close.
lines.say: Why? Demand for US stocks from overseas, and competition from crypto platforms that never close.

lines.text: That plan still depended on final sign-offs and on the price-reporting systems being ready.
lines.say: That plan still depended on final sign-offs and on the price-reporting systems being ready.

lines.text: Now, back to that opening mystery. If most volume skips the exchanges, where does it go?
lines.say: Now, back to the opening mystery. If most volume skips the exchanges, where does it go?

lines.text: Two main places. First, wholesalers: big trading firms that fill orders sent by everyday investors' brokers. They handle most of it.
lines.say: Two main places. First, wholesalers: big trading firms that fill orders sent over by everyday investors' brokers. They handle most of it.

lines.text: Second, dark pools: private trading systems where big investors can trade without showing their orders to the public first.
lines.say: Second, dark pools. Those are private trading systems where big investors can trade without showing their orders to the public first.

lines.text: So when you tap buy in a brokerage app, your order may never reach the NYSE. A wholesaler may fill it instead.
lines.say: So when you tap buy in a brokerage app, your order may never reach the N Y S E at all. A wholesaler may fill it instead.

lines.text: Those trades still get reported, and brokers must seek the best execution reasonably available for your order.
lines.say: Those trades still get reported, and brokers must seek the best execution reasonably available for your order.

lines.text: Chapter 3: How a price gets set.
lines.say: Chapter three: how a price gets set.

lines.text: Every stock has two prices at once. The bid is the most a buyer will pay. The ask is the least a seller will take.
lines.say: Every stock has two prices at once. The bid is the most a buyer will pay. The ask is the least a seller will take.

lines.text: Here's an example quote: a bid of $49.98, and an ask of $50.02.
lines.say: Here's an example quote: a bid of forty-nine dollars and ninety-eight cents, and an ask of fifty dollars and two cents.

lines.text: The gap between them is called the spread. In this example, it's 4 cents.
lines.say: The gap between them is called the spread. In this example, it's four cents.

lines.text: Market makers live on that gap. They post both prices all day, earn the spread, and risk the price moving against them.
lines.say: Market makers live on that gap. They post both prices all day, earn the spread, and risk the price moving against them.

lines.text: Now the orders. A market order says: fill me right now, at whatever the going price is.
lines.say: Now, the orders. A market order says: fill me right now, at whatever the going price is.

lines.text: A limit order says: fill me only at this price or better. If nobody agrees, it may not fill at all.
lines.say: A limit order says: fill me only at this price or better. If nobody agrees to that price, it may not fill at all.

lines.text: And a stop order waits for a trigger price, then turns into a market order.
lines.say: And a stop order waits quietly for a trigger price, then turns into a market order.

lines.text: Back to our example. A market order for 100 shares fills near the ask: 100 x $50.02 = $5,002.
lines.say: Back to our example. A market order for a hundred shares fills near the ask. A hundred times fifty dollars and two cents is five thousand and two dollars.

lines.text: Sell them right back at the bid: 100 x $49.98 = $4,998.
lines.say: Sell them right back at the bid, and a hundred times forty-nine dollars and ninety-eight cents is four thousand, nine hundred ninety-eight dollars.

lines.text: That round trip cost $4, or 0.08% of $5,000, before any fees, even though the price never moved.
lines.say: That round trip cost four dollars, or zero point zero eight percent of five thousand, before any fees, even though the price never moved.

lines.text: A limit buy at $50.00 caps the cost at $5,000. But it only fills if a seller agrees to $50 or less.
lines.say: A limit buy at fifty dollars caps the cost at five thousand dollars. But it only fills if some seller agrees to fifty dollars or less.

lines.text: So it's a trade-off. A market order buys speed. A limit order buys control over the price.
lines.say: So it's a trade-off. A market order buys you speed. A limit order buys you control over the price.

lines.text: So why do prices move at all? When buyers keep taking the ask, sellers raise the ask, and the price climbs.
lines.say: So why do prices move at all? When buyers keep taking the ask, sellers raise the ask, and the price climbs.

lines.text: When sellers keep hitting the bid, buyers lower their bids, and the price falls.
lines.say: And when sellers keep hitting the bid, buyers lower their bids, and the price falls.

lines.text: A stock price is just the last deal two sides agreed on. News, earnings, interest rates and mood all change what people will agree to.
lines.say: A stock price is just the last deal two sides agreed on. News, earnings, interest rates and mood all change what people will agree to.

lines.text: That's also why nobody can promise where a price goes next. It depends on decisions that haven't been made yet.
lines.say: That's also why nobody can promise where a price goes next. It depends on decisions that haven't been made yet.

lines.text: Chapter 4: The scoreboard.
lines.say: Chapter four: the scoreboard.

lines.text: When the news says the market was up, it usually means an index: a scoreboard built from many stocks.
lines.say: When the news says the market was up, it usually means an index. That's a scoreboard built from many stocks at once.

lines.text: The most watched one is the S&P 500: about 500 large U.S. companies, picked by a committee, since 1957.
lines.say: The most watched one is the S and P five hundred: about five hundred large US companies, picked by a committee, since nineteen fifty-seven.

lines.text: To be added, a company needs a market cap of at least $22.7 billion, under rules updated in July 2025.
lines.say: To be added, a company needs a market cap of at least twenty-two point seven billion dollars, under rules updated in July twenty twenty-five.

lines.text: It also has to be based in the U.S., listed on a U.S. exchange, and profitable in its latest quarter and its last four quarters combined.
lines.say: It also has to be based in the US, listed on a US exchange, and profitable, in its latest quarter and its last four quarters combined.

lines.text: Here's the part most people miss: the index is weighted by market cap. Bigger companies count more.
lines.say: Now here's the part most people miss. The index is weighted by market cap, so bigger companies count for more.

lines.text: Example: a $4 trillion company counts 200 times as much as a $20 billion one ($4,000B / $20B = 200).
lines.say: For example, a company worth four trillion dollars counts two hundred times as much as one worth twenty billion.

lines.text: By mid-2026, the 10 largest companies made up about 40% of the S&P 500.
lines.say: By mid twenty twenty-six, the ten largest companies made up about forty percent of the S and P five hundred.

lines.text: Compare that with the dot-com peak in 2000, when the top 10 were about 26%.
lines.say: Compare that with the dot-com peak in two thousand, when the top ten were about twenty-six percent.

lines.text: So in 2026, the scoreboard was far more concentrated than even at the dot-com peak.
lines.say: So in twenty twenty-six, the scoreboard was far more concentrated than even at the dot-com peak.

lines.text: In plain dollars: roughly $40 of every $100 in an S&P 500 index fund sat in just 10 companies.
lines.say: In plain dollars, roughly forty of every hundred dollars in an S and P five hundred index fund sat in just ten companies.

lines.text: The scoreboard at each year's end: about 2,044 in 2015, and about 6,846 in 2025.
lines.say: Here's the scoreboard at each year's end: about two thousand forty-four in twenty fifteen, and about six thousand eight hundred forty-six in twenty twenty-five.

lines.text: But look at 2022. The index fell about 19% that year.
lines.say: But look at twenty twenty-two. The index fell about nineteen percent that year.

lines.text: Then in 2025, it gained about 16.4%, even after a rough spring.
lines.say: Then in twenty twenty-five, it gained about sixteen point four percent, even after a rough spring.

lines.text: Over the long run, the S&P 500 has averaged about 10% a year since 1957, with dividends reinvested, before inflation.
lines.say: Over the long run, the S and P five hundred has averaged about ten percent a year since nineteen fifty-seven, with dividends reinvested, before inflation.

lines.text: But the average hides a lot. Single years often land far from 10%. It's booms and busts, averaged.
lines.say: But the average hides a lot. Single years often land far from ten percent. It's booms and busts, averaged out.

lines.text: And past returns are history. They don't promise anything about the next decade.
lines.say: And past returns are just history. They don't promise anything about the next decade.

lines.text: Chapter 5: Referees and safety nets.
lines.say: Chapter five: referees and safety nets.

lines.text: The top referee is the Securities and Exchange Commission, created by the Securities Exchange Act of 1934.
lines.say: The top referee is the Securities and Exchange Commission, created by the Securities Exchange Act of nineteen thirty-four.

lines.text: Its job, in its own words: "to protect investors; maintain fair, orderly, and efficient markets; and facilitate capital formation."
lines.say: Its job, in its own words, is to protect investors, maintain fair, orderly, and efficient markets, and facilitate capital formation.

scene.text: to protect investors; maintain fair, orderly, and efficient markets; and facilitate capital formation

lines.text: Below the SEC sits FINRA, a nonprofit formed in 2007 to police brokerage firms. The SEC oversees FINRA, too.
lines.say: Below the S E C sits FINRA, a nonprofit formed in two thousand seven to police brokerage firms. And the S E C oversees FINRA, too.

lines.text: Next, settlement. Your trade happens in a blink, but the cash and the shares officially swap later.
lines.say: Next up, settlement. Your trade happens in a blink, but the cash and the shares officially swap hands later.

lines.text: Since May 28, 2024, most U.S. stock trades settle in one business day, called T+1. Before that, it took two.
lines.say: Since May twenty-eighth, twenty twenty-four, most US stock trades settle in one business day, called T plus one. Before that, it took two.

lines.text: One less day means one less day for something to go wrong between buyer and seller.
lines.say: One less day means one less day for something to go wrong between the buyer and the seller.

lines.text: Then there are the emergency brakes, called circuit breakers.
lines.say: And then there are the emergency brakes, called circuit breakers.

lines.text: If the S&P 500 falls 7% from the prior day's close, trading across the whole market stops for 15 minutes.
lines.say: If the S and P five hundred falls seven percent from the prior day's close, trading across the whole market stops for fifteen minutes.

lines.text: At 13%, there's another 15-minute halt. Those two only kick in before 3:25 p.m. Eastern.
lines.say: At thirteen percent, there's another fifteen-minute halt. Those two only kick in before three twenty-five P M Eastern.

lines.text: And at 20%, trading stops for the rest of the day, no matter the time.
lines.say: And at twenty percent, trading stops for the rest of the day, no matter the time.

lines.text: Have they ever fired? Yes. In March 2020, the 7% breaker tripped four times: on the 9th, 12th, 16th and 18th.
lines.say: Have they ever fired? Yes. In March twenty twenty, the seven percent breaker tripped four times: on the ninth, twelfth, sixteenth and eighteenth.

lines.text: Before that, the last market-wide halt came in October 1997, under older rules tied to the Dow.
lines.say: Before that, the last market-wide halt came in October nineteen ninety-seven, under older rules tied to the Dow.

lines.text: Chapter 6: Recap.
lines.say: Chapter six: the recap.

lines.text: One: a share is a slice of a company. After the IPO, the company gets nothing from the trading.
lines.say: One. A share is a slice of a company, and after the I P O, the company gets nothing from the trading.

lines.text: Two: trades happen in many places. In 2025, 50.6% of volume ran off the exchanges, mostly through wholesalers.
lines.say: Two. Trades happen in many places. In twenty twenty-five, fifty point six percent of volume ran off the exchanges, mostly through wholesalers.

lines.text: Three: every price is a bid and an ask. Market orders buy speed, limit orders buy control, and the spread is the toll.
lines.say: Three. Every price is a bid and an ask. Market orders buy speed, limit orders buy control, and the spread is the toll.

lines.text: Four: the S&P 500 is a scoreboard weighted by size, with about 40% in 10 companies by mid-2026.
lines.say: Four. The S and P five hundred is a scoreboard weighted by size, with about forty percent in ten companies by mid twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: And the referees: the SEC and FINRA, one-day settlement, and circuit breakers at 7%, 13% and 20%.
lines.say: And the referees: the S E C and FINRA, one-day settlement, and circuit breakers at seven, thirteen and twenty percent.

lines.text: So the stock market isn't one building on Wall Street. It's buyers and sellers, matched by machines in many places, under one set of rules.
lines.say: So the stock market isn't one building on Wall Street. It's buyers and sellers, matched by machines in many places, under one set of rules.

lines.text: That's the money. Follow for more.
lines.say: That's the money. Follow for more.

post.title: 50.6% of US stock trading skipped the exchanges in 2025. How the market really works
post.ig: In 2025, for the first time, more than half of US stock trading (50.6%) happened off the exchanges. Here's where it went, and how prices really get set.
post.tiktok: In 2025, most US stock trading skipped the exchanges. Here's how the stock market actually works.
post.yt_desc:
How the stock market actually works, from zero: what a share is and why the company gets nothing after its IPO, where trades really happen (in 2025, 50.6% of US stock volume ran off the exchanges, mostly through wholesalers and dark pools), and the planned 23-hour trading day. It walks through a hypothetical bid-ask example ($49.98 bid, $50.02 ask, a $4 round trip on 100 shares), market versus limit orders, how the S&P 500 is built and weighted (about 40% in its top 10 by mid-2026), and the year-end S&P 500 record from 2015 to 2025. It ends with the referees and safety nets: the SEC, FINRA, T+1 settlement since May 28, 2024, and the 7%, 13% and 20% circuit breakers.
